Good morning. The high-level meeting of the General Assembly to commemorate and promote the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons is called to order. Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I warmly welcome all of you to this high-level meeting. Members will recall that by its resolution 68/32 of 5 December 2013, the Assembly declared 26 September as the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. In its resolution 80/49 of 1 December 2025, The General Assembly reiterated its request for the Organization, on 26 September every year, a one-day high-level plenary meeting of the Assembly to commemorate and promote the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. Today, that meeting is being held. In addition, as delegations were informed in my letter dated 17 September 2026, In keeping with the spirit of the General Assembly resolution 72/251, I have invited civil society representatives to make contributions to this meeting. It is my intention to invite these representatives to speak at the end of the morning and afternoon meetings. International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear weapons is devoted to furthering the objective of mobilizing international efforts towards achieving the common goal of a nuclear-weapon-free world, including through enhancing public awareness and education about the threat posed to humanity by nuclear weapons and the necessity for their total elimination. Allow me now to make a statement as President of the General Assembly. Excellencies, Mr. Secretary-General, ladies and gentlemen, 80 years ago, in January 1946, the United Nations General Assembly adopted its very first resolution, in which, among other things, it called for the elimination of atomic weapons from national armaments. It did so months after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, when humanity witnessed their devastating power. The message was unmistakable. Nuclear disarmament is fundamental to humanity's survival. In 1961, President John F. Kennedy warned this very Assembly that every man, woman, and child lives under a nuclear sword of Damocles. capable of being cut at any moment by accident or miscalculation or by madness. The weapons of war must be abolished before they abolish us." More than six decades later, that threat remains as alarming as ever. As of January 2026, the global inventory stood at more than 12,000 nuclear warheads. of particular concern between 2100 and 2200 are kept in a state of high operational alert on ballistic missiles capable of being launched at very short notice. And for the first time since the end of the Cold War, the global stockpile is expected to grow again as new and more modern warheads enter arsenals faster than retired ones are dismantled. Reliance reliance on nuclear deterrence persists. New technologies, including artificial intelligence, cyber capabilities, and advanced delivery systems, are introducing additional uncertainty into command, control, and decision making. Meanwhile, global military expenditure reached nearly $3 trillion in 2025, the 11th consecutive annual increase, diverting resources from sustainable development and human well-being. Taken together, these trends are eroding the guardrails that have helped prevent catastrophe for decades. On 5 February this year, New START expired without a successor. For the first time since 1972, there are no binding limits on strategic nuclear arsenal. The NPT review conference then ended without a consensus outcome, the third consecutive review conference to do so. These are not abstract diplomatic setbacks. They increase the risks of arms racing, escalation, and catastrophic miscalculation. The combination of proliferating conflicts, eroding arms control arrangements, and renewed reliance on nuclear weapons creates a perilous moment for the international peace and security. We must change course urgently and decisively. The starting point must be a simple truth, reaffirmed in the Pact for the Future: A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Risk reduction is urgent, but reducing risk is not a substitute for disarmament. As long as nuclear weapons exist, the danger of their use by design, by accident, or by miscalculation will remain. We therefore need action on four fronts. First, we must restore dialogue and guardrails. I urge the superpowers to return to the negotiating table without delay and agree on a successor framework that restores verifiable limits, transparency, and predictability. All nuclear weapons states must strengthen crisis communication and avoid actions that increase nuclear risks. Second, We must uphold and strengthen the multilateral architecture that has helped to restrain nuclear dangers for decades. The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons remains the cornerstone of global efforts to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, advance nuclear disarmament, and promote cooperation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy. Its three mutually reinforcing pillars must be implemented fully faithfully and without discrimination. The International Atomic Energy Agency is indispensable in this regard. It must receive the cooperation, access and resources needed to carry out its safeguards and verification responsibilities independently and effectively, while continuing to support the peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology. The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty has established a powerful global norm and indispensable global monitoring system. Yet, three decades after it was opened for signature, it has still not entered into force. I urge all States that have not signed or ratified it, particularly the remaining Annex 2 States, to do so without delay and call on all States to maintain the moratorium on nuclear weapons test explosions. Third, we must move from managing arsenals to reducing and eliminating them. Nuclear weapons States must fulfill their disarmament obligations and commitments through concrete, transparent, verifiable and irreversible measures. They should reduce the role of nuclear weapons in security doctrines lower operational readiness, prevent the expansion of arsenals, and honor security assurances, including those connected to nuclear-weapon-free zones. States that have not yet done so should join and comply with relevant disarmament and nonproliferation instruments. We must also support existing nuclear-weapon-free zones and advance new ones on the basis of arrangements freely arrived at by the states concerned. Fourth, we must mobilize people. The purpose of this International Day is not only to commemorate, it is also to educate and mobilize. Survivors, civil society, youth, scientists, and educators keep before us the human cost and the possibility of another path. The voices of the hibakusha and affected communities remind us that nuclear weapons do not distinguish between soldiers and civilians, or between present and future generations. Their testimony must remain central to our work. Excellencies, the history of nuclear disarmament is not only a history of setbacks. It also contains major gains. From a peak of roughly 70,000 warheads in 1986, the global inventory has fallen to about 12,000 today. Nuclear weapons-free zones now cover vast regions of the world. South Africa dismantled its nuclear weapons program. Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Ukraine relinquished their nuclear weapons left on their territories after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. These show that disarmament works when political leaders choose to make it work. Two years ago, through Action 25 of the Pact for the Future, Member States recommitted to the total elimination of nuclear weapons, to strengthen the disarmament and non-proliferation architecture, and to take every possible step to prevent nuclear disaster. Those words must now become policy and practice. If the United Nations is to get back to basics to prevent the scourge of war, then nuclear disarmament must remain our highest disarmament priority, just as it was at the birth of this organization. So let us act with the urgency demanded by the danger, the courage demanded by history, and the responsibility we owe to present and future generations. Let us restore and strengthen the guardrails. Let us reduce the risks. Let us eliminate the weapons. And let us restore trust by building a world free from nuclear weapons. I thank you. I now have the honor to give the floor to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, His Excellency Antonio Guterres. You have the floor, sir.

Mr. President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. We meet at the most dangerous nuclear moment since the end of the Cold War. 81 years after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, nuclear weapons continue to cast a shadow over humanity. And that shadow is darkening. Nuclear arsenals are being expanded and modernized. The rattling of nuclear sabres is growing louder. Advances in technology are increasing the odds of mistake and miscalculation. And just when they are most needed, the safeguards built over decades to contain these dangers are breaking down. Early this year, the New START Treaty expired. For the first time in more than half a century, there are no binding limits on strategic nuclear arsenals. This undermines not only the security of those who possess nuclear weapons, but the entire international community. The 11th Review Conference of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons was unable to reach consensus on a substantive outcome. And the United Nations Disarmament Commission once again completed its three-year cycle without substantive recommendations. These are not simply diplomatic disappointments. They are warning signals. And the lights are flashing red. Rising risks and crumbling guardrails are a one-way ticket to disaster. Excellencies, disarmament is not a favour. It's a binding legal obligation spelled out in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. As we mark this important day, It is time to forge a new path. States possessing nuclear weapons must return to dialogue to prevent any use of nuclear weapon. Maintaining the decades-old reduction in global arsenals is essential to prevent another nuclear arms race. The United States and the Russian Federation must negotiate a successor framework to New START. All nuclear weapons States must reduce the role of nuclear weapons in their security policies, with confidence-building measures that ensure transparency. And in the name of the survivors devastated by nuclear testing, it's beyond time to bring the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty into force. Later this year, Parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons will gather for its first review conference. I welcome this important milestone. Excellencies, these devices of death must never decide the fate of humanity. A divided world cannot be an excuse for inaction. We know the danger and we know the consequences. We know what we have to do to change course. Replace threats with dialogue. Replace arms racing with arms control. Replace paralysis with concrete action. Humanity has lived under the nuclear shadow for more than eight decades. We must ensure that future generations do not. Let us choose a future free from nuclear weapons. I thank you.

Mr. President, I speak on behalf of the Pacific Islands Forum and its 18 members. This day carries profound meaning for our forum family. For the Pacific, nuclear weapons and climate change are not separable challenges. They are interconnected threats to our people, our ocean, and our future. Together, they imperil food security, livelihood, cultural survival, and the human rights of affected communities. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, Kazakhstan is honored to address this Assembly on a day that embodies our shared responsibility to eliminate the gravest threat to humanity, nuclear weapons. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the 12 Pacific Small Island Developing States represented at the United Nations, namely the Federated States of Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Palau, Papua New Guinea, the Republic of Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu, and my own country, Fiji. A majority of our members are also States Parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. These milestones reflect decades of consistent effort by our governments and our peoples towards a world free of nuclear weapons. We note with concern that international momentum has not kept pace. The 2026 Review Conference of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons concluded without a consensus outcome. the third such conservative review conference to do so. President. President Burkina Faso aligns itself with the statement delivered by the Republic of Burundi on behalf of the African Group and that of Uganda on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. First, it is regrettable that three consecutive NPT review conferences have been unable to adopt consensual outcome documents. Cambodia, therefore, calls for the upholding of integrity of the treaty and advancing the three mutual reinforcing pillars. Second, the prolonged delay in bringing the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty into force heightened concern over the political resumption of nuclear testings and risks gradually eroding the confidence in the NPT disarmament pillars. Third, Cambodia reaffirms its commitment to preserving the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon-Free Zones as enshrined in the Treaty. We welcome the nuclear weapons states that have signed the protocol and urge them to ratify it without reservation, while calling on the remaining nuclear weapons states to follow suit. Mr. President, as a peace-loving nation, Cambodia remains convinced that the world is safer without nuclear weapons. We reiterate our call for strengthening multilateral efforts and look forward to the first review conference of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons to be held later this year under the presidency of the Republic of South Africa. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cambodia. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Namibia. You have the floor.

Mr. President, Namibia is honored to host the CTBTO Integrated Field Work Exercise, IFE 26, later this year, the first such exercise on African soil. We look forward to welcoming experts from around the world to contributing to strengthening of comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty verification regime. In conclusion, the message is clear. The total elimination of nuclear weapon is the only way to ensure they are never used. Partial measure, rhetoric, commitment are insufficient. We need renewed political will and the commitment to matter that there is an international transparency and trust. Our collective security depends on it. Our shared humanity demand it. And the best way to honor the victim of nuclear detonation is to ensure that such tragedy are never repeated. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Namibia. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe. You have the floor.

Mr. President, Zimbabwe welcomes the convening of this high-level plenary meeting to commemorate and promote the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. My delegation aligns itself with the statements delivered by the non-aligned movement and the African group. On this occasion, Zimbabwe wishes to underscore that nuclear disarmament remains the highest disarmament priority of the United Nations, as pronounced during the first special session of the General Assembly devoted to disarmament in 1978. Mr. President, Zimbabwe regrets that the 11th Review Conference of the Parties to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, held earlier this year, failed to agree on a consensus outcome. This marked the third consecutive NPT review conference where consensus proved elusive. We are concerned that if this trend continues, it will erode disarmament commitments and chip away at the grand bargain sustaining the three pillars of the NPT: disarmament, non-proliferation and the peaceful uses of nuclear energy. The ongoing qualitative and quantitative nuclear arms race, which appears to be underway, represents a regrettable backsliding from the agreed pathway towards the total, irreversible and verifiable elimination of these dangerous weapons of mass destruction. We call upon all States with nuclear arsenals to commit to the total elimination of their nuclear weapons in accordance with their legal obligations and undertakings under Article VI of the NPT and the various relevant agreed outcomes of previous NPT Review Conferences. We urge nuclear-armed States and other States operating outside these legal regimes to accede to them. I thank the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Philippines. You have the floor, ma'am.

Mr. President, the Philippines aligns itself with the statement delivered by Indonesia on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. More than eight decades after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the catastrophic and irreversible humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons remain the clearest reason for their total elimination. Complete elimination is the only guarantee against their use and is fundamental to global security. Yet, the global trend of nuclear disarmament is gradually being reversed. Some states are reportedly building up their arsenals and undertaking the qualitative development of these weapons. The New START treaty expired in February without a successor. The 11th Review Conference of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons has again ended without consensus for the third consecutive time. The integration of emerging technology into weapons systems compounds existing risk. Nuclear deterrence remains a precarious doctrine. Humanity is best served by the sustained reduction and ultimately the abolition of nuclear arsenals. The Philippines calls for decisive international action, a time-bound, irreversible and verifiable program for the complete elimination of nuclear weapons, with nuclear weapons states and nuclear-capable states outside the NPT being held accountable through concrete benchmarks and structured reporting. Pending this, nuclear weapons states must provide legally binding, unconditional and irrevocable negative security assurances to all non-nuclear weapons states, We reiterate our call for the urgent negotiation and conclusion of a fissile material cut-off treaty and the early entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. We urge all member states to renew their commitment to the NPT, the CTBT, and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. As a state party, the Philippines looks forward to the first review conference of the TPNW later this year. We welcome Timor-Leste's accession to the Bangkok Treaty, which reinforces Southeast Asia's standing as a nuclear-weapon-free zone. Disarmament education, particularly of the youth, must be further mainstreamed to sustain a global culture of peace. Mr. President, no security doctrine can justify the continued existence of nuclear weapons. The Philippines stands ready to work with all Member States towards their total, irreversible and verifiable elimination. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Philippines, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Tonga. You have the floor.

Mr. President, the Kingdom of Tonga aligns itself with the statements delivered on behalf of the Pacific Islands Forum and the Pacific Small Island Developing States, and joins the international community in solemnly commemorating the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons and in reaffirming our shared responsibility to advance the complete elimination of nuclear weapons. For the peoples of our blue Pacific continent, the consequences of nuclear weapons are not confined to history. They remain a solemn and enduring reality that continues to resonate across our region. Our region continues to live with the human and environmental legacy of nuclear testing, a shared experience that compels us to speak with unwavering conviction in defense of peace, human dignity, and justice across generations. On 7 July 2026, Tonga deposited its instrument of ratification of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty and its instrument of accession to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. These actions reaffirmed Tonga's steadfast conviction that international peace and security must rest upon multilateralism, international law, and the complete elimination of nuclear weapons. Tonga reaffirms the enduring importance of the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty and our region's long-standing commitment to a peaceful and nuclear weapon-free Pacific. At a time of heightened geopolitical tensions, we urge all states to renew their commitment to nuclear disarmament and to strengthen the international disarmament architecture. The total elimination of nuclear weapons is a responsibility owe to humanity and to generations yet unborn. Tonga stands ready to continue advancing with conviction the pursuit of a peaceful, secure, and nuclear-weapon-free world. Malo epi to, I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Tonga.

And I give the floor now to the representative of the Kingdom of Morocco.

Thank you, Mr. President. Allow me at the outset to thank you for convening this important meeting, which brings us together around the aspiration that is shared by all of humanity, that is for a world free of the nuclear threat. No health system, no relief mechanism, no humanitarian system in the world would be able to respond to the consequences of a nuclear detonation. That is why the full elimination of these weapons remains the only absolute guarantee against their use. In this spirit, Morocco would like to share four thoughts that might feed into our collective discussions. One, the NPT and the CTPT that were open to signature 30 years ago represent precious assets. Their universalization and respect for the balance between the commitments therein remain the best assurances of their credibility. Two, reliable channels of communications in times of crises, transparency and accountability measures, as well as maintaining human control over all decisions relating to these nuclear weapons, are all practical measures that strengthen the security of us all. 3. Morocco is actively involved in the work of the Middle East Conference for the establishment of a nuclear weapons-free and weapons of mass destruction-free zone, which will be holding its sixth session in 2025. 4. The peaceful uses of nuclear energy, including health, agriculture, water and energy, must fully benefit developing countries. with the essential support of the IAEA and fully in line with security and safety standards. To conclude, the history of disarmament is also one of success. Entire regions have declared themselves free of nuclear weapons and treaties that seemed out of reach now seem to cover almost all of the international community. What the international will has not accomplished in the past can accomplish tomorrow. A world free of nuclear weapons is within our reach and something that we will all be able to hold on to. Thank you. I thank the distinguished representative of the Kingdom of Morocco.
Distinguished representative of South Africa, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. South Africa joins the international community in the commemoration and the promotion of this International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. We associate ourselves with the statements delivered on behalf of the African Group as well as the Non-Aligned Movement. The recent conclusion of the third consecutive review conference on the Non-Proliferation Treaty without agreement on a consensus outcome document means that it is more important than ever that we act in the common interest of all States and humanity, in unity and urgency, to pursue our goal of a nuclear-weapon-free world. The lack of progress in implementing long-overdue obligations and previous commitments under the NPT is putting a strain on the nuclear disarmament architecture. South Africa deeply regrets that nuclear weapons continue to feature prominently in the military and security doctrines and policies of a select group of states. Profound tensions in the geopolitical environment, heightened by the unabated expansion and modernization of nuclear arsenals, the increasing salience of nuclear weapons in military and security doctrines, as well as research in nuclear rhetoric and threats are matters of grave concern and a timely reminder of the urgency of realizing a world free of nuclear weapons. Mr. President, the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, the TPNW, is an important additional instrument that strengthens our efforts towards a nuclear-weapon-free world. The convening of the first review conference of States Parties to the TPNW later this year provides the opportunity to strengthen the implementation of this historic treaty that brought into force a comprehensive legal prohibition of nuclear weapons as a necessary and effective measure towards the cessation of the nuclear arms race and a path to nuclear disarmament. The steady advance of the TPNW should provide additional impetus for progress on other key elements of the global nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation architecture, including towards the coming into force of the CTBT and the strengthening of nuclear-weapon-free zones. We seize this opportunity as President of the First Review Conference of the TPNW to commend all countries that have signed and ratified the Treaty and invite all those who have not yet done so to consider signing and ratifying the treaty without any further delay. I thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa.

And I give the floor now to the honorable representative of Egypt.

Sayyida Rais.

Mr. President, Egypt reaffirms that this day represents an opportunity to renew the international commitment to the complete elimination of nuclear weapons, given the existential threat they pose to humanity, their danger to international peace and security, and their catastrophic environmental, health, and humanitarian consequences. Thus, my delegation wishes to underscore the following five messages. First, the importance of addressing nuclear weapons from a comprehensive perspective aimed at their total elimination, in parallel with banning nuclear testing, eliminating fissile materials, adopting an all-first-use policy, and providing legally binding and unconditional security assurances to non-nuclear weapon States. Complete elimination achieved in a transparent, irreversible, verifiable manner and within a specified time frame remains the only effective guarantee for the implementation of the obligations of nuclear weapons states under Article VI of the NPT. Second, the serious concern arising from the recent justifications advanced within the disarmament machinery to prevent nuclear weapon states from implementing their obligations, including concepts such as deterrence or strategic stability, as well as notions of responsible nuclear weapon states or nuclear proliferation among friendly states. In this regard, Account must be taken of the impact of such justifications and concepts on efforts to implement the purpose and objectives of the NPT, while emphasizing that confidence-building and risk-reduction measures cannot serve as a substitute for a comprehensive, legally binding agreement on total nuclear disarmament. Third, the need to renew full commitment to the NPT as the cornerstone of the global disarmament and non-proliferation regime with all its three pillars. Egypt expresses disappointment at the failure of the last three review conference cycles, most recently in April 2026. We note that the reason for this failure lies in the lack of genuine political will on the part of nuclear weapon states to implement their obligations. Fourth, the urgent need to continue efforts towards the establishment of a zone free of nuclear weapons and all other WMDs in the Middle East, while taking into consideration that the region remains one of the clearest manifestations of the imbalance resulting from the non-universality of the NPT. So this undermines trust and confidence and risks triggering an arms race in the region. Fifth and finally, Egypt underscores the added value of the conference convened by the UN pursuant to GA decision 73/546 on the establishment of a Middle East zone free of nuclear weapons and WMDs. We look forward to the upcoming session in November. Thank you.

I would like to thank His Excellency, the representative of Egypt.

Distinguished representative of Trinidad and Tobago, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Trinidad and Tobago joins the international community in commemorating the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. This observance serves as a solemn reminder of the catastrophic humanitarian, environmental, and developmental consequences that can result from the use of nuclear weapons. For Trinidad and Tobago, a small island developing state firmly committed to multilateralism, international peace and security, the existence of nuclear weapons remains incompatible with humanity's aspirations for a safer, more just and sustainable world. The continued possession and modernization of nuclear arsenals, coupled with growing geopolitical tensions, underscores the urgent need to reinforce efforts towards disarmament and non-proliferation. Trinidad and Tobago reaffirms its unwavering support for the objectives of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and welcomes initiatives aimed at advancing effective, verifiable and irreversible nuclear disarmament. We also reiterate our strong commitment to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which represents an important step towards delegitimizing nuclear weapons and advancing the goal of their complete elimination. As a member of the Caribbean community and a proud party to the Treaty of Tlatelolco, Trinidad and Tobago remains committed to preserving Latin America and the Caribbean as a nuclear-weapon-free zone. We believe that such regional arrangements contribute significantly to international peace and security and demonstrate that collective security can be achieved without reliance on nuclear deterrence. Today, we call upon all states, particularly those possessing nuclear weapons, to fulfill their disarmament obligations and commitments through meaningful dialogue. confidence-building measures, and concrete actions that reduce nuclear risks and advance the complete elimination of nuclear arsenals. In the midst of heightened geopolitical tensions and mounting security challenges, we must renew our commitment to meaningful dialogue, diplomacy, and multilateral cooperation to fulfill the very first mandate of the United Nations. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Trinidad and Tobago, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Myanmar. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, we are gathering today against the backdrop of increased nuclear weapons spending, heightened risks to nuclear safety, expanded nuclear sharing and proliferation. At the same time, the trust deficit in multilateral institutions and collective security architecture is rising. Mr. President, a single use of nuclear weapons, whether by design or accident, will have catastrophic humanitarian and environmental consequences. Therefore, the only guarantee against the use or non-threat of use of nuclear weapons is their total elimination. NPT remains the cornerstone of nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation. The continued failure to adopt an outcome document at the past three consecutive review conferences is deeply alarming. Myanmar attaches great importance to the universal adherence to the CDBT and calls upon all States that have not ratified the CDBT, especially the remaining NS2 States, to do so without delay for its entry into force. We are of the view that the TPNW complements NPT and strengthens the nuclear disarmament regime. After the expiration of the New START Treaty, Myanmar underscores the need to pursue good faith negotiations for a successful agreement. Mr. President, Myanmar ratified the CTBT and signed the TPNW to advance our shared goal of total elimination of nuclear weapons. Unfortunately, Our subsequent plan to ratify the TPNW was disrupted by the 2021 military coup. In the same way, peace and stability in our country was also disrupted following the escalations of violence by the military junta, including aerial attacks, shelling, artillery attacks, and weaponization of dual-use items against civilians. Just yesterday, the military hunter carried out a deadly airstrike on a local market in Chaung Taung, Rakhine State, killing at least 49 people, including women and children, and injuring many. The military hunter that disregard innocent lives of civilians cannot be trusted to pursue civilians or peaceful aspect of dual use item in good faith. In this context, we are seriously concerned with the ongoing collaborations between the military junta and a major nuclear weapon state on their so-called nuclear power plant. Any international assistance of cooperation in nuclear power, even under peaceful use, should only resume in Myanmar when peace and stability are rebuilt, democracy is genuinely restored, and the military is under civilian oversight. Taking this opportunity, I appeal all member states to cut the flows of arms, weapons, jet fuel, and dual-use items to the military junta to save lives of the people of Myanmar.
I thank the distinguished representative of Myanmar. And I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. We are today at a deeply concerning moment for nuclear disarmament. More than eight decades after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, nuclear weapons continue to occupy a central place in security doctrines of a number of states. Rather than moving towards their elimination, we are witnessing more modernization and expansion of arsenals and growing reliance on nuclear deterrence arrangements. The international community cannot accept this trajectory as a new normal. We face a crisis of compliance and credibility. Article 6 of the NPT established a legal obligation that is neither optional nor conditional upon favorable geopolitical circumstances. Yet, implementation of the treaty remains profoundly imbalanced. No nuclear weapons states have accepted permanent and verifiable non-proliferation obligations, while there is no progress towards nuclear disarmament by nuclear-armed states. The failure of the 11th NPT Review Conference to agree on a substantive outcome is a matter of concern to us all. It was not merely another diplomatic setback. It exposed persistent disagreements over the implementation of the treaty and the widening gap between commitments and action. The credibility of the NPT depends on implementation, on nuclear-armed countries being faithful to their commitments. We must also rebuild arms control, reduce and hopefully eliminate the role of nuclear weapons, and return to serious negotiations on disarmament. The normalization of nuclear rhetoric and policies that broaden the role of nuclear weapons in security doctrines are deeply troubling. Nuclear sharing arrangements and their possible expansion is also alarming. A non-proliferation regime cannot sustainably seek to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons while tolerating the spread of dependence upon them. Mr. President, Latin America and the Caribbean chose another path. Through the Treaty of Tlatelolco, our region demonstrated that security can be strengthened by rejecting nuclear weapons. This was also the path taken by other nuclear-weapon-free zones across the globe. Such arrangements must be valued, strengthened, and emulated. Brazil remains convinced that the only lasting guarantee against the use of nuclear weapons is their complete, irreversible and verifiable elimination. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil. And as indicated by the President of the General Assembly, our last speaker for the morning session will be a representative of civil society. The United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, China, Israel, India, Pakistan, and North Korea. No disarmament negotiations, not even modest risk reduction measures. Instead, they are squandering more than $100 billion a year enhancing and expanding their apocalyptic arsenals. For the first time since the end of the Cold War, the total number of nuclear weapons is rising, 12,000 doomsday devices and counting. But these nine nations are not alone in perpetuating nuclear dangers. A few dozen of their allies aid and abet this madness, stationing foreign nuclear forces on their territories, welcoming them into their ports and airfields, and promoting the delusional doctrine of nuclear deterrence.
